Front: What is a generic class and what problem does it solve?
Back: A class with one or more type parameters that provides compile-time type safety for any type without duplicating code.
Extra: Without generics you would need `StringBox`, `IntBox`, etc. or use `Object` with unsafe casts. With generics: `Box<String> b = new Box<>("hello");` — the compiler rejects `new Box<String>(42)` immediately.

Front: Show the full declaration of a two-field generic class `Pair<K,V>`.
Back: `class Pair<K,V> { private final K key; private final V value; public Pair(K key, V value) { this.key=key; this.value=value; } public K getKey() { return key; } public V getValue() { return value; } }`
Extra: Usage: `Pair<String, Integer> p = new Pair<>("age", 30);` — the compiler infers types in the diamond `<>` on the right-hand side (Java 7+).

Front: How does a generic method differ from a method on a generic class?
Back: A generic method introduces its own type parameters (before the return type) and is independent of any class-level type parameters.
Extra: `public static <T> List<T> repeat(T item, int times) { ... }` — this can be on a non-generic class and is callable as `repeat("x", 3)` or explicitly `MyUtil.<String>repeat("x", 3)`.

Front: What is the failure mode of implementing a raw generic interface?
Back: Compile-time generic safety is lost. The compiler cannot check argument types and will only emit unchecked warnings, not errors.
Extra: `class Broken implements Comparable { public int compareTo(Object o) { ... } }` — now `broken.compareTo(42)` compiles even if `Broken` should only compare to other `Broken` instances.

Front: How does `<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>` restrict a type parameter?
Back: `T` must be both a `Number` subclass and implement `Comparable<T>`. Inside the method, you can call `Number` methods and use `compareTo`.
Extra: `public static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T clamp(T val, T min, T max) { if (val.compareTo(min) < 0) return min; if (val.compareTo(max) > 0) return max; return val; }` — the class bound (`Number`) must come before interface bounds.

Front: What can you do inside a `<T extends Number>` method that you cannot do with plain `<T>`?
Back: Call `Number` instance methods on the `T` value — e.g. `n.doubleValue()`, `n.intValue()` — without casting.
Extra: `public static <T extends Number> double sum(List<T> list) { double total = 0; for (T n : list) total += n.doubleValue(); return total; }` — without the bound, `n.doubleValue()` is a compile error.

Front: Explain what `<?>` means and when to use it.
Back: An unbounded wildcard — the list holds some unknown type. Use it when you only need to read elements as `Object` and the algorithm is completely type-agnostic.
Extra: `void printAll(List<?> list) { for (Object o : list) System.out.println(o); }` — works for `List<String>`, `List<Integer>`, etc. Cannot add elements: `list.add("x")` is a compile error.

Front: Why can't you add elements to a `List<? extends Number>`?
Back: Because `? extends Number` is an unknown subtype of `Number`. The actual element type could be `Integer`, `Double`, or `Long`. Adding an `Integer` to what might be a `List<Double>` would be type-unsafe.
Code: List<? extends Number> nums = new ArrayList<Double>(); nums.add(1); // COMPILE ERROR` — the compiler rejects this to prevent heap pollution. You can only read: `Number n = nums.get(0);

Front: Why can you add `Integer` values to a `List<? super Integer>`?
Back: Because `? super Integer` is some type that can hold an `Integer` — it must be `Integer`, `Number`, or `Object`. Any of those can store an `Integer`, so the add is safe.
Extra: `List<? super Integer> list = new ArrayList<Number>(); list.add(1); list.add(2);` — reading, however, returns only `Object`: `Object o = list.get(0);` because the actual type above `Integer` is unknown.

Front: Explain the PECS rule and its purpose.
Back: PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) tells you which wildcard to choose: use `extends` when reading (producing values), use `super` when writing (consuming values).
Extra: `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` — `src` produces T (you read it → extends), `dest` consumes T (you write into it → super). If both reading and writing are needed, use the exact type `T`.

Front: How does `Stream.map(Function<? super T, ? extends R>)` illustrate PECS?
Back: `? super T` — the function consumes `T` (input). `? extends R` — the function produces `R` (output). This lets you pass a `Function<Number, Integer>` to a `Stream<Integer>.map(...)`.
Extra: `Stream<Integer> ints = Stream.of(1,2,3); Stream<String> strs = ints.map(Object::toString); // Function<? super Integer, ? extends String>` — the extra flexibility avoids requiring an exact `Function<Integer, String>`.

Front: Describe what type erasure does step-by-step.
Back: 1. Replace every type parameter with its upper bound (or `Object`). 2. Insert explicit casts at every typed retrieval. 3. Generate bridge methods where needed for polymorphism.
Extra: `List<String> names = ...; String s = names.get(0);` becomes `List names = ...; String s = (String) names.get(0);` in bytecode. The cast is inserted automatically; if something wrong is in the list, `ClassCastException` occurs here.

Front: Why does `void process(List<String> l)` and `void process(List<Integer> l)` cause a compile error?
Back: After erasure both have signature `void process(List l)` — identical. The JVM cannot distinguish them so the compiler rejects the overload.
Extra: This is a common surprise. The fix is to rename one method or consolidate into a single `void process(List<?> l)` if the body can work with any type.

Front: What is a raw type and when is it unavoidable?
Back: A generic class used without type arguments (e.g. `List` instead of `List<String>`). It is technically unavoidable only inside `instanceof` checks, because `instanceof List<String>` is a compile error.
Extra: `if (obj instanceof List) { List<?> list = (List<?>) obj; ... }` — switch to `List<?>` immediately after the check to restore at least the null-safety of wildcards. Never assign to a raw `List`.

Front: Show the three work-arounds for the "cannot create generic array" limitation.
Back: Option 1: use `List<T>`. Option 2: `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked") T[] arr = (T[]) new Object[n];`. Option 3: `T[] arr = (T[]) Array.newInstance(clazz, n);` with a `Class<T>` token.
Extra: Option 2 is common inside generic containers like `ArrayList`. Option 3 is used when you must expose a typed array (e.g. `toArray(T[])` implementations). The unchecked warning in option 2 is safe only if `arr` never escapes to unparameterized code.

Front: How do you instantiate a type parameter `T` inside a generic class?
Back: You cannot write `new T()`. Pass a `Class<T> clazz` to the constructor and call `clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`.
Code: class Factory<T> { private Class<T> clazz; Factory(Class<T> clazz) { this.clazz = clazz; } T create() throws Exception { return clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); } }` — usage: `new Factory<>(MyService.class).create();

Front: Why can generics not use primitive types like `int`?
Back: Generics are implemented via `Object` references; after erasure, `T` becomes `Object`. Primitives are not objects and cannot be stored in `Object` slots.
Extra: `List<int> nums = new ArrayList<>(); // COMPILE ERROR` Use `List<Integer>` instead. Autoboxing and unboxing handle the conversion automatically: `nums.add(1)` boxes to `Integer`; `int n = nums.get(0)` unboxes. For performance-critical code, consider `int[]` directly.

Front: What is a bridge method and why does the compiler generate it?
Back: A synthetic method generated by the compiler to preserve polymorphism when a subclass implements a generic interface with a specific type.
Extra: `class StringComparator implements Comparator<String>` — the compiler generates a bridge `compare(Object, Object)` that delegates to `compare(String, String)`. This way the JVM's polymorphic dispatch works even though the bytecode erases `String` to `Object`.

Front: Difference between `<T extends Number>` (bounded parameter) and `<? extends Number>` (wildcard)?
Back: Bounded parameter `<T>` gives the type a name — use it when you reference the type multiple times (e.g. input and output must both be `T`). Wildcard `<?>` is anonymous — use it in method parameters when you only read and do not need to name the type.
Extra: `<T extends Number> T clamp(T v, T min, T max)` — same type everywhere. `void printAll(List<? extends Number> list)` — you read `Number` but don't care about the exact subtype and don't return it.

Front: How do generic collections use wildcards in utility methods?
Back: `Collections.sort(List<T> list)` requires `T extends Comparable<? super T>` — the `? super T` allows a `Comparator<Number>` to sort a `List<Integer>`. The wildcard ensures the utility works for subtypes of the bound too.
Extra: `List<Integer> ints = Arrays.asList(3,1,2); Collections.sort(ints); // Integer implements Comparable<Integer>` — but also `Collections.sort(List<Number>)` works if `Number` happened to implement `Comparable<Number>`, thanks to the `? super T` bound.
